node.label: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein
node.date_label: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) · The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983) · Divine Art, Infernal Machine (2011)
node.description: In The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), Elizabeth L. Eisenstein argued that the shift from manuscript to print transformed the conditions of learning in early modern Europe. Identical printed copies could circulate widely and be compared, helping reshape the Renaissance, the Reformation and the rise of modern science. It is still cited, in DeLacy’s words, as “the seminal work in the cultural history of the book.” Roger Chartier praised the synthesis while questioning the breadth of its explanatory ambition in 1981. Bruno Latour used its account of print in his work on inscriptions, while objecting that the invention of printing itself remained unexplained. The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe (1983) abridged the larger study; Divine Art, Infernal Machine (2011) examined changing, often ambivalent attitudes toward printing.

proposed_edges.relationship: Latour’s “Visualisation and Cognition” (1986) uses Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) to develop his account of mobile, stable inscriptions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author manuscript pp. 10–12, section C: “mobilization and immutability”; sustained discussion follows. Selected manuscript, not a collation of 1986/1990 versions; Eisenstein’s complete book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Visualisation and Cognition” (1986), Latour objects that Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) leaves the invention of printing itself unexplained.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author manuscript pp. 12–13: “does not account for the technical innovations themselves.” Distinct criticism within his positive uptake; same version limits as ee_w_01.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) in 1981, Chartier calls Eisenstein’s long-term synthesis powerful but questions its ambition to encompass Western society’s transformations since the fifteenth century.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review p. 192: “sa force” and “sa démesure.” Only pp. 191–192 read; no more specific later objection asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Power and excess of the synthesis

proposed_edges.relationship: Chartier’s 1981 review contrasts Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979), which stresses the manuscript-to-print transition, with Goody’s emphasis on the oral-to-written transition.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: p. 192, paragraph beginning “La première, celle des anthropologues”: named comparison by Chartier. Goody’s particular title is not specified there; originals unread; no personal exchange or influence inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) explains how the circulation and comparison of printed materials helped transform early modern science.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge description explicitly names the rise of modern science; full book unread. Latour’s selected discussion corroborates this reading, but does not independently verify the historical cases.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) is “still cited as the seminal work in the cultural history of the book,” as Margaret Eisenstein DeLacy wrote in 2016; a 2007 collection, Agent of Change: Print Culture Studies after Elizabeth L. Eisenstein, took stock of the work that followed it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). The cited UMass Press page returned 403 to me (WebFetch and curl), so the 'catalytic role' description could not be read. DeLacy's AHA obituary (read) supports a narrower claim. Note that DeLacy writes as a family member (Margaret Eisenstein DeLacy); the claim is attributed to her. Add ee_w_delacy2016 to source_ids. Phrase seen: “"It is still cited as the seminal work in the cultural history of the book."; "Among the most meaningful was Agent of Change: Print Culture Studies after Elizabeth L. Eisenstein (2007)"” Read at: https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/elizabeth-eisenstein-april-2016/

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Rise of the Writer” (1979), Robert Darnton drew upon Elizabeth L. Eisenstein’s The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) to explain how multiplying and standardizing texts changed literature as a mode of communication.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Darnton’s discussion of literary communication on the magazine’s own site, especially the paragraph beginning “Narrative intended directly”. He explains the consequences of standardized, multiplied texts and explicitly attributes that analysis to Eisenstein’s articles and her 1979 book. This is an affirmative use of her argument within his review of John Lough’s Writer and Public in France, rather than a review of Eisenstein’s book. It supports this specific uptake, not a general claim that all of Darnton’s book history derives from Eisenstein.

proposed_edges.relationship: Bert Hogenkamp’s 2004 review reports that, in A Social History of the Media (2002), Peter Burke and Asa Briggs weigh Eisenstein’s print-revolution thesis in The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979) against its critics, noting that defenders of the thesis too easily forget the survival of oral culture while declining to take sides.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete Hogenkamp review on the journal publisher’s PDF, pp. 143–145. Its sustained discussion names Eisenstein and her book, then explains how Burke and Briggs treat her revolution thesis alongside oral continuity and contextual approaches. The reviewer emphasizes that they see merits on both sides and preserve the long-term explanatory value of the revolution approach. This is a qualified critique reported by a reviewer, not wholesale rejection. The underlying book passage was not read: its licensed preview displayed a viewing restriction. Credit is shared with Asa Briggs; the endpoint is Burke alone because Briggs has no eligible timeline endpoint. This is substantive engagement with Eisenstein, not an edge inferred from textbook co-credits.
